# Access as code

![](../images/spot-5.svg){.spot fig-alt="A gate with a yellow lintel, three pods and a sheet of paper on a mint tile. An elephant in a vest checks a clipboard."}
Roles and grants are often typed into a database by hand. Keeping them in
code puts the rules in a file, which can be audited later on. The lab uses Pulumi and pgsesame for access as code.
Pulumi compares its program with a state file, while pgsesame keeps no state and reads the server's catalog
every time it plans.

## The access model

Both tools describe the same model:

- two group roles, `app_ro` (read) and `app_rw` (read and write), that cannot log in
- usage on the schema, and grants on its tables and sequences, for the group roles
- **default privileges**, so that tables the `app` role creates later get the same grants (the part
  that hand-made setups most often forget)
- two login users, `reporter` and `ingest`, who get access only through membership in a group role

Tables, schemas and extensions stay out of the model, because they belong to the application and its
migrations.

## Pulumi {#pulumi-state-and-a-diff}

`pulumi/__main__.py` builds the model with `pulumi-postgresql`, a bridge to the provider that
Terraform uses. `pulumi preview` shows what would change, and `pulumi up` applies it:

```bash
pulumi preview            # what would change
pulumi up
pulumi preview --refresh  # drift check: re-read the database first
```

A plain `preview` compares the program with the state file and leaves the database alone, which is
why changes made by hand appear only with `--refresh`. The grants also have to be chained with
`depends_on`, because the provider runs them in parallel and Postgres then fails with "tuple
concurrently updated".

## pgsesame {#pgsesame-one-yaml-file-no-state}

[pgsesame](https://github.com/almostly/pgsesame) declares the same model in `pgsesame/spec.yaml`. Its
`plan` command reads the database catalog and prints the SQL that would make the server match the
spec:

```yaml
principals:
  app_ro:
    type: role
    privileges:
      schemas: {usage: [public]}
      tables: {select: [public.*]}
  reporter:
    type: user
    password_env: SESAME_REPORTER_PASSWORD
    member_of: [app_ro]

default_privileges:
  - owner: app
    schema: public
    grantee: app_ro
    tables: [select]
```

```bash
sesame plan     # exit code 2 means there are changes
sesame apply    # one transaction: 32 statements on a fresh server
sesame plan     # empty: nothing drifted
sesame import   # write a spec from what a server grants today
```

Destructive changes (revokes, drops and changes of owner) need explicit flags, and passwords come
from environment variables instead of the file.

## Pulumi and pgsesame compared

| | Pulumi | pgsesame |
|---|---|---|
| source of truth | a Python program plus a state file | one YAML spec |
| drift | detected with `--refresh` | every plan reads the database |
| apply | resources in parallel, chained by hand | one transaction |
| scope | anything with a provider, databases and beyond | Postgres roles and privileges |
| secrets | encrypted in stack config | environment variables |

Either tool works, as long as only one of them manages the roles on a given server. Pulumi fits when
database access is one part of a larger infrastructure program, and pgsesame fits when the database
is the whole concern and the plan should be readable SQL.
